newsitem.title: USA: U.S. promises to boost aid to Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. promises to boost aid to Lebanon.

text.p: The United States pledged on Monday to step up aid to Lebanon, including increased training of Lebanese military and law enforcement officers.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher announced the moves as he opened a one-day conference at the State Department of potential donors to Lebanon, devastated by a 16-year civil war that ended in 1991.

He told delegates from some 30 countries and eight international financial institutions that Lebanon needed help with its economic and social infrastructure, private sector and security forces. "The United States intends to help in each of the three areas," he said.
-- increase its assistance for basic infrastructure, agricultural development, education and training and social services;
-- work to expand the flow of goods, services and capital between the U.S. and Lebanese private sectors;
-- bolster training of Lebanese military and law enforcement officers and continue to provide non-lethal military equipment.

Christopher gave no figures but Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri has said he would ask the delegates, known as the "Friends of Lebanon," for contributions of up to $5 billion for reconstruction projects in the next five years.
Christopher made no mention in his address of lifting a long-standing U.S. ban on travel to Lebanon by U.S. citizens, nor was the subject raised in brief opening remarks by Hariri.

Washington insists the ban is purely a security matter dating back to the seizure of American hostages by pro-Iranian groups in the 1980s. But Beirut suspects it is being used as a lever to force it into signing a peace treaty with Israel.

Christopher reaffirmed support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Lebanon and the "ultimate" withdrawal of all foreign forces. Both Israeli and Syrian forces are currently stationed in various parts of the country.

He paid tribute to Hariri for the "great strides" Lebanon had made under his leadership but said more needed to be done to help Lebanon "resume its traditional role as a dynamic trading centre for the entire region."

He also said he remained hopeful that Israel-Palestinian negotiations over the West Bank town of Hebron would succeed despite the slow progress they were making. "The negotiations over Hebron in the last two months have certainly been very difficult but nevertheless I remain optimistic that a final agreement will soon be reached", Christopher said.
"In recent months Palestinians and Israelis have been in particular reminded that negotiation is the only real alternative to renewed violence," he said.

Israel and the Palestinians have been negotiating since October over a partial Israeli troop withdrawal from the town as required under the Oslo peace accords. But they have bogged down over details of future security arrangements.
